explanations.C: Necrosis with loss of AQP4-positive astrocytes and complement deposition is the pathology of neuromyelitis optica.
explanations.D: Mitotic figures with pseudopalisading necrosis would indicate glioblastoma, the tumor this biopsy was performed to exclude.
explanations.E: Symmetric pontine myelin loss with minimal inflammation is the pattern of osmotic demyelination syndrome.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman reports 5 days of pain around her left eye that worsens with eye movement and blurred central vision; she says red objects look washed out with that eye. Two years ago she had tingling in both legs that resolved over several weeks. When a light is swung from the right eye to the left eye, both pupils dilate. Which fundoscopic finding is most likely in the left eye?

answers.A: Bilateral disc swelling with peripapillary hemorrhages

explanations.A: Bilateral disc swelling with peripapillary hemorrhages indicates papilledema from raised intracranial pressure, which is typically painless with preserved acuity early.
explanations.B: A cherry-red spot with retinal whitening indicates central retinal artery occlusion, which causes sudden painless monocular vision loss.
explanations.C: Copper wiring with arteriovenous nicking indicates chronic hypertensive retinopathy in a patient with long-standing high blood pressure.
explanations.D: Optic neuritis, often a presenting feature of MS, is usually retrobulbar, so despite painful eye movement, red desaturation, and a relative afferent pupillary defect, the disc appears normal in most patients (mild swelling in about one-third).
explanations.E: Venous engorgement with widespread hemorrhages indicates central retinal vein occlusion, which causes painless vision loss.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis takes the first dose of a new once-daily oral disease-modifying therapy in clinic under continuous ECG monitoring. Varicella zoster IgG was confirmed positive before treatment. She remains asymptomatic, and her heart rate and ECG findings are shown. In addition to periodic lymphocyte counts and liver enzymes, which adverse effect requires specific screening during the first months of this therapy?

explanations.A: First-dose bradycardia and AV block identify fingolimod, an S1P receptor modulator that can also cause macular edema, so an ophthalmologic exam is recommended at baseline and 3–4 months after starting.
explanations.B: Drug-induced lupus is associated with hydralazine, procainamide, and isoniazid, not S1P receptor modulators.
explanations.C: Hemorrhagic cystitis is caused by the acrolein metabolite of cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide.
explanations.D: Peripheral neuropathy is characteristic of vinca alkaloids, isoniazid, and metronidazole rather than fingolimod.
explanations.E: Sensorineural hearing loss is associated with aminoglycosides, cisplatin, and loop diuretics.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a sore throat. She arrives in a sequined evening dress, hugs the physician on entering, and describes her symptoms as 'the most unbearable agony anyone has ever felt' but cannot give specific details. She refers to the nurse she met 5 minutes earlier as her closest friend and shifts from tears to laughter within moments. When the physician answers a page, she sulks and raises her voice to regain attention. She has no history of self-harm and does not take advantage of others. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Borderline personality disorder features abandonment fears, unstable identity, and self-harm, which are absent in this patient.
explanations.B: Dependent personality disorder involves submissiveness and need for reassurance rather than attention-seeking theatrics.
explanations.C: Needing to be the center of attention, seductive dress, shallow and rapidly shifting emotions, impressionistic speech, and perceiving relationships as more intimate than they are define histrionic personality disorder.
explanations.D: Narcissistic personality disorder centers on grandiosity, entitlement, and exploitation of others rather than emotional display.
explanations.E: Schizotypal personality disorder involves magical thinking and eccentric behavior rather than dramatic attention-seeking.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man reports a year of headaches and says his wedding ring and shoes no longer fit. He has coarse facial features and a prominent jaw. He recently had two minor car accidents after failing to see vehicles approaching from either side. Laboratory results are shown. Which visual field defect is most likely on formal testing?

explanations.A: A GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma extends superiorly to compress the optic chiasm, where the crossing nasal retinal fibers carry the temporal visual fields, producing loss of peripheral vision on both sides.
explanations.B: Left homonymous hemianopia results from a right optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, or complete right optic radiation lesion.
explanations.C: Left monocular blindness results from a left optic nerve lesion anterior to the chiasm.
explanations.D: Right inferior quadrantanopia results from a lesion of the left parietal optic radiations (Baum loop).
explanations.E: Right superior quadrantanopia results from a lesion of the left temporal optic radiations (Meyer loop).

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman begins outpatient therapy after an emergency department visit for superficial cuts to her forearm following a breakup. She describes chronic feelings of emptiness and frantic efforts to avoid being abandoned. At her first session she tells the therapist, 'You are the only person who has ever understood me.' Two weeks later, after the therapist reschedules an appointment, she calls the therapist 'cruel and completely useless.' Which of the following defense mechanisms best explains her change in attitude toward the therapist?

explanations.A: Displacement redirects emotions from their true source to a safer target, such as yelling at a spouse after being criticized by a boss.
explanations.B: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable impulses to others, as in a patient who is angry accusing others of being hostile.
explanations.C: Reaction formation replaces an unacceptable impulse with its opposite, such as excessive kindness toward someone one resents.
explanations.D: Alternating idealization and devaluation of the same person, viewing others as all good or all bad, is splitting, the characteristic defense of borderline personality disorder.
explanations.E: Sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities and is considered a mature defense.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago has had progressive right-sided weakness, word-finding difficulty, and a right visual field defect over 5 weeks. He is afebrile. MRI shows multiple asymmetric T2-hyperintense lesions in the left subcortical and periventricular white matter without enhancement or mass effect. Laboratory studies are shown. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

answers.B: CSF JC virus DNA by PCR

explanations.A: Cryptococcal antigen testing identifies cryptococcal meningitis, which presents with headache, fever, and elevated opening pressure rather than focal non-enhancing white matter lesions.
explanations.B: Subacute progressive focal deficits with non-enhancing white matter lesions lacking mass effect in a patient with a CD4 count far below 200/µL indicate PML, which is confirmed by detecting JC virus DNA in CSF by PCR.
explanations.C: Oligoclonal bands support MS, a relapsing disease of young adults, not progressive multifocal deficits in advanced AIDS.
explanations.D: Aquaporin-4 IgG confirms neuromyelitis optica, which targets the optic nerves and spinal cord that PML typically spares.
explanations.E: Toxoplasma encephalitis in AIDS causes ring-enhancing lesions with edema and mass effect, and IgG seropositivity alone does not confirm active disease.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man is brought to the physician by his sister because of personality changes. Eight months ago he fell from scaffolding and sustained bilateral frontal lobe contusions. Before the injury he was a reliable foreman with no legal problems. Since then he makes crude jokes at inappropriate times, spends money impulsively, and has outbursts at minor frustrations, but he sleeps 7 hours nightly and his speech is not pressured. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.B: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic
answers.E: Personality change due to brain injury

explanations.A: Antisocial personality disorder requires a long-standing pattern with evidence of conduct disorder before age 15, whereas his behavior began only after the injury.
explanations.B: A manic episode would include decreased need for sleep and pressured speech, which he lacks, and would not be explained by a clear temporal link to frontal trauma.
explanations.C: Borderline personality disorder is an enduring pattern of instability evident by early adulthood across settings, not a new change after a brain injury at age 34.
explanations.D: Intermittent explosive disorder describes recurrent aggressive outbursts that are not better explained by another medical condition such as frontal lobe injury.
explanations.E: A clear temporal and physiologic relationship between frontal contusions and new disinhibition in a previously well-functioning adult indicates personality change caused by a medical/neurologic condition.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis uses a daily subcutaneous injection. One morning, within minutes of injecting, she develops flushing, chest tightness, palpitations, and shortness of breath that resolve spontaneously within 15 minutes. Examination shows several areas of lipoatrophy at prior injection sites. By which mechanism does this drug reduce relapses?

answers.D: Diverts T cells toward a myelin-like decoy

explanations.A: Nrf2 activation is the mechanism of dimethyl fumarate, an oral agent whose flushing is not accompanied by injection-site lipoatrophy.
explanations.B: Blocking leukocyte integrin adhesion is natalizumab's mechanism, given as a monthly IV infusion rather than a daily injection.
explanations.C: CD20-positive B-cell depletion describes ocrelizumab, a twice-yearly infusion whose reactions occur during the infusion.
explanations.D: Glatiramer acetate is a polymer of glutamate, alanine, tyrosine, and lysine that resembles myelin and acts as a decoy for the immune response; its classic adverse effects are injection-site reactions and a transient post-injection flushing and chest-tightness reaction.
explanations.E: Inhibition of pyrimidine synthesis via DHODH is teriflunomide's mechanism, an oral agent that causes hepatotoxicity and alopecia.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman has sudden, severe, painful vision loss in both eyes and, 3 weeks later, develops paraplegia, a T4 sensory level, and urinary retention. A similar episode of vision loss 2 years ago left her with poor visual recovery. Brain MRI shows no periventricular lesions. Spinal MRI shows a central T2-hyperintense lesion extending from T1 to T8. CSF oligoclonal bands are absent. Biopsy of the spinal cord lesion would most likely show which finding?

answers.E: Symmetric myelin loss with minimal inflammation

explanations.A: In neuromyelitis optica, anti-aquaporin-4 IgG binds astrocyte water channels and activates complement, producing necrotizing demyelination with complement deposition and loss of AQP4-positive astrocytes, consistent with her severe bilateral optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis.
explanations.B: Enlarged oligodendrocytes with viral inclusions indicate PML, which usually spares the optic nerves and spinal cord and occurs in immunosuppressed patients.
explanations.C: Perivenous lymphocytic sleeves of demyelination are seen in ADEM, a monophasic post-infectious illness with encephalopathy.
explanations.D: Plaques with relative axonal preservation are typical of MS, whose cord lesions are usually short and accompanied by periventricular lesions and oligoclonal bands.
explanations.E: Symmetric myelin loss with minimal inflammation describes osmotic demyelination syndrome, which centers on the pons after rapid sodium correction.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician after two episodes of rhythmic jerking of his left hand that lasted 1 minute each without loss of consciousness. He is otherwise well, and neurologic examination between episodes is normal. Stereotactic biopsy of a lesion in the right frontal lobe later shows a WHO grade 2 diffuse astrocytoma. Which of the following preoperative MRI findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?

answers.A: Dural-based enhancing mass with a dural tail
answers.B: Multiple enhancing masses at the gray-white junction
answers.C: Nonenhancing T2-hyperintense mass with minimal edema
answers.D: Ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and edema
answers.E: Smooth ring enhancement with central restricted diffusion

explanations.A: A dural-based, extra-axial enhancing mass with a dural tail is characteristic of meningioma.
explanations.B: Multiple enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction suggest hematogenous metastases.
explanations.C: Low-grade gliomas appear as well-defined masses that are T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense with no significant enhancement and little surrounding edema, reflecting an intact blood-brain barrier.
explanations.D: Irregular ring enhancement with central necrosis and marked edema is typical of high-grade glioma (glioblastoma).
explanations.E: A smooth ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion suggests a pyogenic brain abscess.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man is evaluated for right arm weakness that began 2 months ago during a febrile illness with meningitis attributed to West Nile virus. His legs have normal strength and reflexes, plantar responses are flexor bilaterally, and sensation is intact throughout. Findings from his upper extremity examination are shown. Where is the lesion most likely located?

explanations.A: A left internal capsule lesion causes contralateral UMN weakness with increased tone and reflexes and no fasciculations.
explanations.B: A left primary motor cortex lesion causes contralateral UMN weakness with hyperreflexia rather than atrophy and fasciculations.
explanations.C: A right lateral corticospinal tract lesion produces ipsilateral UMN signs below the level, including hyperreflexia and involvement of the leg.
explanations.D: The ventral corticospinal tract controls axial and proximal musculature bilaterally, and its injury produces subtle UMN deficits rather than focal atrophy.
explanations.E: West Nile virus can destroy anterior horn cells, and loss of LMN cell bodies at C5–C6 produces weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, decreased tone, and an absent biceps reflex at that level only.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman had an episode of left optic neuritis 14 months ago that resolved completely over 6 weeks. She now presents with numbness and clumsiness of her right hand that developed over 3 days. MRI shows an enhancing lesion in the cervical cord and several non-enhancing periventricular lesions. Her hand symptoms resolve fully over the next month, and she had no residual deficits or worsening between the two episodes. Which pattern best describes her disease course?

explanations.A: Clinically isolated syndrome describes a single first demyelinating episode lasting at least 24 hours; her second attack at a new site moves her beyond this category.
explanations.B: Primary progressive MS worsens continuously from onset without distinct relapses and remissions.
explanations.C: Radiologically isolated syndrome refers to MS-like MRI lesions found incidentally in a person who has never had clinical symptoms.
explanations.D: Relapsing-remitting MS is defined by discrete attacks of new neurologic symptoms followed by partial or complete recovery with stability between relapses, as in this patient.
explanations.E: Secondary progressive MS begins as relapsing-remitting disease but later worsens steadily independent of relapses, which has not occurred here.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis reports brief electric shock-like sensations that shoot down her spine and into her legs whenever she bends her neck forward. She also has intermittent paroxysms of stabbing pain in her right cheek lasting seconds. Neurologic examination between episodes is normal, and MRI shows a demyelinating plaque in the cervical cord. These positive symptoms are best explained by which mechanism?

explanations.A: Ca2+ overload from reversed Na+/Ca2+ exchange causes axonal degeneration and fixed deficits, not brief paroxysmal sensations with a normal interictal examination.
explanations.B: Conduction block across bare internodes produces negative symptoms such as numbness, weakness, or vision loss rather than spontaneous electric sensations.
explanations.C: Without myelin insulation, adjacent bare axons excite one another (ephaptic transmission) and fire ectopically, producing positive symptoms such as Lhermitte sign and trigeminal neuralgia.
explanations.D: Retrograde neuronal loss reflects chronic neurodegeneration and causes progressive disability and atrophy, not movement-triggered paroxysms.
explanations.E: Upper motor neuron disinhibition produces spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign, which are motor findings rather than sensory paroxysms.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis notes that her fatigue and blurred vision in her previously affected right eye worsen during hot yoga classes and on humid summer days, then return to baseline within an hour of cooling off. MRI shows no new lesions. She wants to remain physically active. Which nonpharmacologic recommendation is most likely to reduce these episodes?

answers.B: Complete bed rest for several weeks

explanations.A: Aerobic and strength training reduce MS fatigue, so exercise should continue with a start-low, go-slow approach that avoids overheating.
explanations.B: Prolonged bed rest causes deconditioning, which is itself a secondary cause of fatigue.
explanations.C: Heat further impairs conduction in demyelinated axons with a reduced safety factor (Uhthoff phenomenon), so cooling vests, cold drinks, and air conditioning reduce heat-related fatigue and transient symptoms.
explanations.D: Hot baths and showers raise core temperature and would worsen her heat-sensitive symptoms.
explanations.E: Caffeine is not a recommended MS fatigue strategy and can disrupt sleep, worsening secondary fatigue.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia reports sudden, painless loss of vision in his right eye that developed over seconds 1 hour ago. He has a right relative afferent pupillary defect and a right carotid bruit. Fundoscopy shows whitening of the retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea, narrowed arterioles with segmented blood columns, and a bright yellow refractile body at an arteriolar bifurcation. What is the most likely source of the occlusion?

explanations.A: A refractile yellow Hollenhorst plaque is a cholesterol embolus from ipsilateral carotid atherosclerosis that lodges in the central retinal artery, causing ischemic retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot at the fovea.
explanations.B: Cavernous sinus thrombosis causes painful proptosis, chemosis, and ophthalmoplegia from involvement of CN III, IV, VI, and V1.
explanations.C: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes bilateral papilledema with headaches that develop over weeks to months.
explanations.D: Left atrial myxoma can embolize but produces tumor emboli with constitutional symptoms, not refractile cholesterol plaques in a patient with a carotid bruit.
explanations.E: Vertebral artery dissection causes posterior circulation ischemia that produces homonymous field defects rather than monocular retinal ischemia.

questions.question: A 49-year-old man has had multiple sclerosis for 17 years. His early relapses resolved completely, but he now has a fixed spastic paraparesis that has not improved, and recent MRI shows no enhancing lesions. MRI does show T1-hypointense "black holes" and cerebral atrophy. In his chronically demyelinated axons, voltage-gated Na+ channels have redistributed along the bare membrane, causing persistent Na+ influx. Which process most directly converts this change into irreversible axonal loss?

answers.B: JC virus lytic infection of oligodendrocytes
answers.E: Reversed Na+/Ca2+ exchange with Ca2+ overload

explanations.A: Complement-mediated destruction of AQP4-positive astrocytes is the mechanism of neuromyelitis optica, driven by anti-aquaporin-4 IgG.
explanations.B: Lytic JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes causes PML in severely immunosuppressed patients, not chronic axonal loss in long-standing MS.
explanations.C: Methylmalonic acid accumulation in vitamin B12 deficiency disrupts myelin synthesis in the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
explanations.D: Osmotic oligodendrocyte apoptosis follows overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia and causes osmotic demyelination syndrome.
explanations.E: Persistent Na+ entry reverses the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and the resulting intra-axonal Ca2+ overload, compounded by lost oligodendrocyte metabolic support, destroys the axon and causes permanent disability.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man develops 3 days of burning pain over his left forehead followed by a vesicular rash on an erythematous base involving the left forehead, upper eyelid, and tip of the nose. His left eye is red and tearing. Involvement of the nasal tip indicates a high risk of corneal involvement because the virus has reactivated along which nerve?

explanations.A: The frontal nerve is a V1 branch that supplies the forehead and scalp via the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves but not the cornea or nasal tip.
explanations.B: The infraorbital nerve is a V2 branch supplying the cheek, lower eyelid, and upper lip, so vesicles there would not predict corneal disease.
explanations.C: The lacrimal nerve is a V1 branch supplying the lateral upper eyelid and conjunctiva near the lacrimal gland, not the nasal tip.
explanations.D: The nasociliary nerve (V1) gives rise to the long ciliary nerves that carry corneal pain and touch sensation and to the external nasal branch supplying the nasal tip, so vesicles there (Hutchinson sign) predict keratitis.
explanations.E: The zygomatic nerve is a V2 branch supplying the lateral cheek and temple and carrying parasympathetic fibers toward the lacrimal gland.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden headache, vomiting, and right-sided weakness while shoveling snow. At a rural urgent care center, a skull radiograph is obtained and interpreted as normal, and he is transferred to a stroke center 90 minutes after symptom onset. Examination shows right hemiparesis and aphasia. Findings on arrival are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.B: Obtain noncontrast CT of the head
answers.D: Perform lumbar puncture with CSF analysis
answers.E: Repeat skull radiographs in six hours

explanations.A: Thrombolysis cannot be given until intracranial hemorrhage is excluded, and sudden headache with vomiting and severe hypertension strongly suggests hemorrhage.
explanations.B: Noncontrast CT has replaced skull radiography for intracranial pathology and rapidly shows acute intracerebral hemorrhage as a hyperdense parenchymal lesion, which must be distinguished from ischemic stroke before treatment.
explanations.C: MRI is more sensitive for early ischemia but is slower and less practical than CT for the initial emergent exclusion of hemorrhage, and contrast is not required.
explanations.D: Lumbar puncture is used when subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected despite a negative CT and is dangerous before imaging in a patient with focal deficits.
explanations.E: Skull radiographs are limited to findings such as depressed fractures or hardware and cannot detect parenchymal lesions, so repeating them adds nothing.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man who emigrated from Vietnam 10 years ago was recently diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. His neurologist recommends a disease-modifying therapy given as an intravenous infusion twice yearly that kills its target cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytolysis and complement-mediated lysis. Pretreatment screening results are shown, and the infusion is postponed pending hepatology evaluation. Which medication was most likely planned?

explanations.A: Alemtuzumab also lyses lymphocytes via antibody- and complement-dependent cytotoxicity, but it is given as annual courses and its hallmark risk is secondary autoimmunity.
explanations.B: Glatiramer acetate is a daily or three-times-weekly subcutaneous injection that acts as a myelin decoy, with no need to defer for hepatitis B.
explanations.C: Interferon beta-1a is self-injected and causes flu-like symptoms, depression, and liver enzyme elevation, but it is not a twice-yearly infusion.
explanations.D: Natalizumab is a monthly infusion that blocks α4-integrin rather than lysing cells, and its key pretreatment test is JC virus antibody status.
explanations.E: Ocrelizumab is an anti-CD20 antibody infused every 6 months that depletes B cells, and active hepatitis B (positive HBsAg) is a contraindication because B-cell depletion can cause fulminant HBV reactivation.

questions.question: A 49-year-old man with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has taken a once-daily oral medication for 6 years. When he started, he required 6 hours of heart-rate monitoring after the first dose, and an eye examination 3 months later was normal. He now has a pearly, telangiectatic papule with rolled borders on his nose, and biopsy confirms basal cell carcinoma. His neurologist notes that periodic skin examinations are recommended with this medication. Which medication is he most likely taking?

explanations.A: Fingolimod requires first-dose cardiac monitoring for bradycardia/AV block and ophthalmologic screening for macular edema, and it increases the risk of skin cancers such as basal cell carcinoma, melanoma, and squamous cell carcinoma.
explanations.B: Glatiramer acetate is a subcutaneous injection that causes injection-site and post-injection reactions without cardiac monitoring requirements.
explanations.C: Interferon beta-1a is an injectable associated with flu-like symptoms, depression, and cytopenias rather than skin cancer.
explanations.D: Natalizumab is a monthly intravenous infusion whose major risk is JC virus–associated PML.
explanations.E: Teriflunomide is oral but does not require first-dose cardiac monitoring; its key risks are hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 'mood swings.' Her mood shifts from intense anger to despair within a few hours, usually after arguments with her boyfriend, whom she alternately adores and despises. She describes chronic emptiness, impulsive spending, binge eating, and frantic calls to her boyfriend whenever he goes out without her. She has cut her thighs on several occasions. She has never had a period of elevated mood lasting several days, and her sleep is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Instability of relationships, self-image, and affect with mood reactivity lasting hours, abandonment fears, emptiness, impulsivity, and self-harm meets at least 5 criteria for borderline personality disorder.
explanations.B: Cyclothymic disorder involves at least 2 years of fluctuating hypomanic and depressive symptoms lasting days, not reactive shifts lasting hours.
explanations.C: Histrionic personality disorder involves attention-seeking and shallow emotions but not self-harm, emptiness, or abandonment fears.
explanations.D: Major depressive disorder requires at least 2 weeks of persistently depressed mood rather than brief interpersonal mood reactivity.
explanations.E: Rapid-cycling bipolar disorder requires at least 4 discrete mood episodes per year, with hypomania lasting at least 4 days and decreased need for sleep, which she lacks.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motorcycle crash. He has left periorbital swelling, and CT shows a fracture of the lesser wing of the left sphenoid bone that extends through the left optic canal. Extraocular movements are full. Which visual finding is most likely on examination?

explanations.A: Bitemporal hemianopia results from injury to the optic chiasm, which lies above the pituitary gland rather than within the optic canal.
explanations.B: Left homonymous hemianopia results from a right retrochiasmal lesion that affects both eyes.
explanations.C: The optic nerve enters the cranium through the optic canal carrying all visual fibers from one eye before any cross at the chiasm, so injury here causes ipsilateral monocular vision loss with a left afferent pupillary defect.
explanations.D: Right homonymous hemianopia results from a left optic tract, lateral geniculate, or radiation lesion behind the chiasm.
explanations.E: Right monocular vision loss would require injury to the right optic nerve, which travels through the right optic canal.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis begins a twice-daily oral disease-modifying therapy. Within the first 2 weeks she develops episodes of facial warmth, redness, and itching about 30 minutes after each dose, along with abdominal pain and diarrhea; the flushing lessens when she takes aspirin beforehand. Her liver enzymes and ECG are normal. Which mechanism best describes how this drug reduces CNS inflammation?

explanations.A: α4-integrin blockade is natalizumab's mechanism, a monthly IV infusion that does not cause dose-related flushing.
explanations.B: CD20-positive B-cell depletion describes ocrelizumab, which causes infusion reactions rather than flushing after oral doses.
explanations.C: Dimethyl fumarate modifies Keap1 to activate Nrf2 antioxidant signaling and suppress inflammatory signaling, reducing oxidative stress, T-cell activity, and microglial activation; its prostaglandin-mediated flushing is blunted by aspirin.
explanations.D: DHODH inhibition of pyrimidine synthesis is teriflunomide's mechanism, whose adverse effects include alopecia and hepatotoxicity rather than flushing.
explanations.E: S1P receptor–mediated lymphocyte sequestration is fingolimod's mechanism, which causes first-dose bradycardia rather than flushing.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis received two annual courses of an intravenous anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody, the second 20 months ago. She now presents with gum bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, and petechiae on her shins. She is afebrile, has no new neurologic findings, and her spleen is not palpable. Laboratory results are shown. Which mechanism best explains her thrombocytopenia?

explanations.A: Disseminated intravascular coagulation would produce schistocytes and abnormal coagulation studies in an acutely ill patient.
explanations.B: Direct marrow suppression would lower multiple cell lines during or shortly after drug exposure, not cause isolated thrombocytopenia 20 months later.
explanations.C: Thrombotic microangiopathy such as TTP produces schistocytes and often renal dysfunction, fever, and neurologic changes, none of which are present.
explanations.D: After alemtuzumab-induced lymphocyte depletion, B cells repopulate faster than regulatory T cells, producing secondary autoimmunity such as immune thrombocytopenia from antiplatelet autoantibodies, with isolated thrombocytopenia and large platelets.
explanations.E: Splenic sequestration requires splenomegaly, usually from portal hypertension, and her spleen is not palpable.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis undergoes biopsy of an atypical enhancing lesion. Staining at the lesion edge shows depletion of a glial cell type with a round nucleus surrounded by a clear perinuclear halo, each of which normally myelinates internodes on many different axons. Over the following months, repeat MRI shows partial recovery of the lesion. The new myelin in this lesion is most likely produced by cells derived from which population?

explanations.A: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help produce and circulate CSF; they do not generate myelin.
explanations.B: Schwann cells derive from neural crest and myelinate a single internode of one peripheral axon; they do not normally remyelinate CNS plaques.
explanations.C: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells persist in the adult CNS and are the only source of new oligodendrocytes for remyelination after the "fried egg" oligodendrocytes are destroyed.
explanations.D: Reactive astrocytes form the dense gliotic scar of chronic plaques rather than producing new myelin.
explanations.E: Satellite glial cells surround neuronal cell bodies in peripheral sensory and autonomic ganglia and do not myelinate axons.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of 8 months of progressive difficulty walking. He takes short, shuffling steps as if his feet are stuck to the floor, has developed urinary incontinence, and has become slow to answer questions. He has no tremor or rigidity. MRI of the brain shows markedly enlarged lateral ventricles with only mild widening of the cortical sulci. Which of the following interventions is most likely to improve his symptoms?

explanations.A: Carbidopa-levodopa treats Parkinson disease, which presents with resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia rather than magnetic gait with incontinence and ventriculomegaly.
explanations.B: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used for Alzheimer disease, in which ventricular enlargement is proportional to diffuse cortical atrophy (hydrocephalus ex vacuo).
explanations.C: The triad of magnetic gait, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline with ventricles enlarged out of proportion to sulci indicates normal pressure hydrocephalus, which can improve with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
explanations.D: Thiamine treats Wernicke encephalopathy, which presents acutely with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia rather than ventriculomegaly.
explanations.E: B12 replacement treats subacute combined degeneration with dorsal column and corticospinal tract signs and does not cause ventricular enlargement.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of right face and arm weakness and nonfluent speech. On examination, both eyes are conjugately deviated to the left, and he cannot voluntarily move his eyes to the right. Damage to which structure best explains his eye findings?

explanations.A: The left frontal eye field (MCA territory, rostral to the motor cortex) normally drives the contralateral right PPRF for rightward gaze, so its loss leaves the intact right frontal eye field unopposed and the eyes deviate toward the lesion, consistent with the accompanying aphasia and right hemiparesis.
explanations.B: A left MLF lesion causes a left INO with failed left eye adduction on rightward gaze, not a conjugate deviation.
explanations.C: A left oculomotor nucleus lesion causes ptosis and a down-and-out left eye, and it lies in the midbrain rather than MCA territory.
explanations.D: A right abducens nucleus lesion can cause a rightward gaze palsy, but a right pontine lesion would produce left-sided weakness and no aphasia.
explanations.E: A right PPRF lesion would also impair rightward gaze, but it lies in basilar territory and could not explain aphasia with right-sided weakness.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician with her sister. She cannot choose what to order at a restaurant or what to wear without calling her sister first, and she agreed to move across the country with her former husband despite not wanting to because she feared losing his support. Two weeks after her divorce she moved in with a man she had just met because she felt helpless living alone. She describes herself as incapable and lacking confidence. Which of the following features best distinguishes her condition from avoidant personality disorder?

answers.B: Fear of criticism and social disapproval
answers.E: Seeking care and reassurance from others

explanations.A: Inhibition in and avoidance of new social situations is characteristic of avoidant personality disorder.
explanations.B: Fear of criticism, disapproval, and rejection is the core feature of avoidant personality disorder.
explanations.C: Feelings of inadequacy are shared by both avoidant and dependent personality disorders and therefore do not distinguish them.
explanations.D: Seeing oneself as socially inept or unappealing is a feature of avoidant personality disorder.
explanations.E: Although both disorders feel inadequate, dependent personality disorder is defined by a need to be taken care of, with difficulty making decisions without reassurance and urgently seeking a new relationship when one ends.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who works as an accountant comes to the physician because of loneliness. She says she would love to have close friends and a partner but turns down invitations from coworkers because she is sure they will find her boring and awkward. She only spends time with people when she is certain they already like her and avoids speaking in meetings for fear of saying something foolish. Which of the following features best distinguishes her condition from schizoid personality disorder?

answers.D: Magical thinking with odd speech patterns
answers.E: Suspicion that others intend to cause harm

explanations.A: In avoidant personality disorder the patient wants relationships but avoids them because of fear of rejection, whereas in schizoid personality disorder the desire for relationships is absent.
explanations.B: Emotional coldness and detachment is characteristic of schizoid personality disorder, not avoidant personality disorder.
explanations.C: Indifference to praise or criticism is a schizoid feature; avoidant patients are hypersensitive to criticism.
explanations.D: Magical thinking and odd speech characterize schizotypal personality disorder.
explanations.E: Pervasive suspicion that others intend harm is the hallmark of paranoid personality disorder.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history reports 2 months of pain radiating from his left shoulder down the medial arm. He has mild left ptosis, decreased sweating on the left side of his face, and a left pupil that is smaller than the right, with the difference most pronounced in dim light. Chest x-ray shows a left apical lung mass. The postganglionic fibers that normally dilate his left pupil reach the eye through which nerve?

explanations.A: The chorda tympani carries CN VII taste fibers from the anterior tongue and parasympathetics to the submandibular ganglion.
explanations.B: The greater petrosal nerve carries CN VII preganglionic parasympathetics to the pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimation.
explanations.C: Sympathetic fibers ascend the chain to the superior cervical ganglion and then ride with the long ciliary nerves (branches of V1) to the dilator pupillae, so a Pancoast tumor interrupting this chain causes miosis that is most obvious in the dark.
explanations.D: The oculomotor nerve carries parasympathetic constrictor fibers, and its injury produces a dilated rather than constricted pupil.
explanations.E: The short ciliary nerves carry postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion to the sphincter pupillae.

questions.question: A 45-year-old surgeon is hospitalized for an elective procedure. He insists that only the department chair is qualified to examine him and belittles the resident as 'unworthy of my time.' Colleagues report that he routinely presents junior surgeons' research as his own to secure awards, expects to be operated on first, and becomes enraged when his judgment is questioned. Which of the following features of his personality disorder best distinguishes it from histrionic personality disorder?

answers.A: Entitled exploitation of others for status
answers.B: Fear of abandonment with recurrent self-harm
answers.C: Perception of relationships as more intimate
answers.D: Seductive behavior used to draw attention

explanations.A: Narcissistic personality disorder is defined by superiority, need for admiration, and entitlement, and exploitation of others is prominent, whereas histrionic patients tend toward emotional display and rarely exploit others.
explanations.B: Abandonment fears with self-harm are characteristic of borderline personality disorder.
explanations.C: Perceiving relationships as more intimate than they really are is a feature of histrionic personality disorder.
explanations.D: Sexually seductive behavior to gain attention is a histrionic feature.
explanations.E: Theatrical, shallow, rapidly shifting emotions are the hallmark of histrionic personality disorder.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man comes to the emergency department after a new-onset focal seizure. He reports 2 weeks of worsening headache and low-grade fevers. One month ago he had a molar extraction complicated by a dental infection. He is HIV negative. Examination shows mild left pronator drift. Laboratory and MRI findings are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
table: Single right frontal lesion with thin, smooth ring enhancement
Restricted diffusion within the lesion core

explanations.A: Glioblastoma also ring-enhances but has a thick, irregular wall with central necrosis that does not restrict diffusion, and fever with a recent dental infection is not expected.
explanations.B: Low-grade astrocytoma is T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense with no significant enhancement and little edema.
explanations.C: Metastases are usually multiple lesions at the gray-white junction and occur in patients with a known primary tumor.
explanations.D: A single smooth, thin-walled ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion (pus) and edema after a contiguous dental infection, with fever and leukocytosis, indicates a pyogenic brain abscess.
explanations.E: Toxoplasmosis causes multiple ring-enhancing lesions, typically in the basal ganglia, in patients with advanced HIV (CD4 < 100/mm³), and this patient is HIV negative.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis started a self-administered intramuscular disease-modifying injection 4 months ago. She reports fever, chills, and muscle aches lasting about a day after each injection. Over the past month she has lost interest in activities, sleeps poorly, and has had thoughts that her family would be better off without her. Laboratory results are shown. The therapeutic benefit of this medication in multiple sclerosis is best attributed to which mechanism?

answers.A: Blockade of leukocyte migration across the blood-brain barrier
answers.B: Competitive decoy for myelin-reactive T cells
answers.D: Reduced antigen presentation and T-cell activation
answers.E: Sequestration of lymphocytes within lymph nodes

explanations.A: Blocking leukocyte migration across the blood-brain barrier via α4-integrin is natalizumab's mechanism, which causes PML rather than flu-like symptoms and depression.
explanations.B: Acting as a decoy for myelin-reactive immune cells is the mechanism of glatiramer acetate, which causes injection-site and post-injection reactions.
explanations.C: Complement-mediated B-cell lysis describes ocrelizumab, an infusion that causes infusion reactions and infections rather than depression.
explanations.D: Interferon beta-1a binds its receptor to trigger a transcriptional response that reduces antigen presentation and T-cell proliferation, alters cytokine and MMP expression, and restores suppressor function; its adverse effects include flu-like symptoms, depression/suicidality, liver enzyme elevation, and cytopenias.
explanations.E: Lymphocyte sequestration in lymph nodes is the mechanism of fingolimod, an oral agent associated with bradycardia and macular edema.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis at age 31 after a series of relapses that each resolved almost completely. Over the past 5 years he has had no discrete attacks, yet his gait has steadily deteriorated and he now walks with a cane. His Expanded Disability Status Scale score has risen from 2.0 to 5.5 over this period. MRI shows no enhancing lesions and progressive brain atrophy. Which pattern best describes his current disease course?

explanations.A: Clinically isolated syndrome describes only a first demyelinating event, not decades of disease with multiple relapses.
explanations.B: Primary progressive MS worsens from onset without a preceding relapsing phase, whereas this patient had years of relapses that remitted.
explanations.C: Radiologically isolated syndrome describes incidental MS-like MRI lesions in someone who has never had symptoms.
explanations.D: Relapsing-remitting MS is characterized by discrete attacks with recovery and stability between them, not continuous relapse-free decline.
explanations.E: Secondary progressive MS follows an initial relapsing-remitting phase with continuous worsening of neurologic function that occurs independently of relapses, as in this patient.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has visual evoked potentials showing a markedly prolonged P100 latency in the left eye. Recordings from a demyelinated axon segment show that passive depolarizing current decays over a much shorter distance than normal, so less current reaches the next node of Ranvier. A change in which passive property of the bare internodal membrane best explains this finding?

explanations.A: Axial resistance depends on axon diameter and cytoplasm rather than myelin, so it is not the property altered by loss of the sheath.
explanations.B: A higher length constant would let current spread farther passively, the opposite of what occurs after demyelination.
explanations.C: Higher membrane resistance is the effect of intact myelin, which lengthens the length constant and speeds conduction.
explanations.D: Lower membrane capacitance is also a property of intact myelin; demyelination raises capacitance, so more charge is needed to depolarize the membrane.
explanations.E: Loss of myelin lowers membrane resistance so current leaks out across bare internodes, shortening the length constant and slowing or blocking conduction to the next node.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and two relapses in the past year is considering a disease-modifying therapy. A pharmaceutical representative states that the drug 'reduces disability progression by a quarter.' The neurologist checks the trial data shown. Which value is the relative risk reduction for disability progression with Drug Y?

explanations.A: 10% is the absolute risk reduction (0.40 − 0.30), not the reduction relative to the control rate.
explanations.B: CER = 320/800 = 0.40 and EER = 240/800 = 0.30, so RRR = ARR/CER = 0.10/0.40 = 25%, matching the representative's claim.
explanations.C: 30% is simply the experimental event rate (240/800), not a measure of risk reduction.
explanations.D: 33% results from mistakenly dividing the ARR by the experimental rather than the control event rate (0.10/0.30).
explanations.E: 75% is the relative risk (EER/CER = 0.30/0.40); the RRR equals 1 minus this value.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis began a once-daily oral medication 6 months ago; his first dose required 6 hours of cardiac monitoring because of bradycardia. He feels well and has had no infections. Routine laboratory studies show an absolute lymphocyte count of 380/µL (reference 1,000–4,800/µL) with normal hemoglobin, neutrophil, and platelet counts. Which mechanism best explains his lymphopenia?

answers.E: Oxidative apoptosis of activated T cells

explanations.A: Complement-mediated lymphocyte lysis occurs with CD20- or CD52-targeted monoclonal antibodies such as ocrelizumab and alemtuzumab, not an oral agent.
explanations.B: Impaired pyrimidine synthesis via DHODH inhibition is teriflunomide's mechanism, which limits activated lymphocyte proliferation but does not cause first-dose bradycardia.
explanations.C: Fingolimod is a functional antagonist of S1P receptors that internalizes S1P1 on lymphocytes, preventing their egress from lymph nodes and lowering circulating counts, while S1P effects on atrial myocytes explain first-dose bradycardia.
explanations.D: Marrow suppression would typically reduce multiple cell lines and is a toxicity of interferons or cytotoxic chemotherapy rather than S1P modulation.
explanations.E: Oxidative stress pathways are modulated by dimethyl fumarate, which activates Nrf2 and causes lymphopenia without first-dose bradycardia.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman with highly active relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and a 38-year-old man with mild, infrequently relapsing disease are both offered the same infusion therapy. Their neurologist reviews two trials of the drug conducted in different populations, shown below, and notes that far fewer highly active patients must be treated to prevent one relapse. Which measure of efficacy is identical in the two trials?

explanations.A: ARR is 0.30 in Trial 1 but only 0.05 in Trial 2, because absolute benefit scales with baseline risk.
explanations.B: The control event rate is 0.60 versus 0.10, reflecting the different baseline disease activity of the two populations.
explanations.C: The experimental event rate is 0.30 versus 0.05, so it differs between the trials.
explanations.D: NNT is about 4 (1/0.30 ≈ 3.3) in Trial 1 but 20 (1/0.05) in Trial 2, which is why fewer highly active patients must be treated.
explanations.E: RRR is 0.30/0.60 = 50% in Trial 1 and 0.05/0.10 = 50% in Trial 2; relative effects can stay constant even when absolute benefit differs with baseline risk.
